title: Khedivate of Egypt
capsule: The Khedivate of Egypt was an autonomous tributary state of the Ottoman Empire, created in 1867 when Sultan Abdülaziz granted Isma'il Pasha of the Muhammad Ali dynasty the hereditary title of Khedive. Isma'il's costly modernisation drive — railways, telegraphs, expansion into the Sudan, and the Suez Canal (opened 1869) — was financed by ruinous borrowing that produced European financial control and, after the Urabi revolt, British military occupation in 1882. The Khedivate persisted under continued British oversight and nominal Ottoman suzerainty until 1914, when Britain declared a protectorate, deposed Abbas II, and installed Hussein Kamil as sultan.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Egypt's boundaries during the Khedivate period are well attested by Ottoman administrative records and European consular surveys; the Nile Valley core is precisely mapped, though the Sudanese and Libyan frontier zones were less formally demarcated.
